clinicalPearls: The sinus node sits at the lateral-superior junction of the right atrium and superior vena cava, within the upper portion of the crista terminalis where the smooth posterior wall (from the sinus venosus) meets the trabeculated anterior right atrium.

Normal sinus rhythm runs between roughly 60 and 100 beats/min, with a sinus P wave that is upright in leads II, III, and aVF, negative in aVR, and initially positive/biphasic in V1, reflecting an inferiorly and leftward-directed frontal-plane axis.

Sinus arrhythmia is a common, usually asymptomatic finding defined as a sinus-origin rhythm with P-P interval variation greater than 120 ms; when P-wave morphology also varies, premature atrial contractions rather than true sinus arrhythmia are the likely cause.

Three patterns of sinus arrhythmia are described: respirophasic (vagal tone reflexively falls in inspiration and is restored in expiration), ventriculophasic (seen with heart block or after a PVC, where an interposed ventricular beat shortens the P-P interval), and nonphasic (P-P variation unrelated to cardiac or respiratory cycle).

Sinus tachycardia (>100 beats/min) arises from sympathetic stimulation and/or vagal withdrawal; the earliest activation focus shifts more leftward toward the superior septal crista terminalis, producing taller inferior-lead P waves than in resting sinus rhythm.
Sinus bradycardia is defined as a rate <60 beats/min but can be entirely normal during sleep and in physically fit individuals.
A gradual rate rise with an identifiable trigger (such as exertion) favors sinus tachycardia, whereas abrupt onset and offset favor focal atrial tachycardia originating near the sinus node.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is an uncommon disorder of autonomic dysregulation in which the sinus rate climbs at rest or out of proportion to physiologic demand; it most often affects women in their third or fourth decade.
POTS is defined by symptomatic sinus tachycardia on standing, with a rate increase of at least 30 beats/min or to >120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of hypotension.
POTS can follow a viral illness and may resolve spontaneously over 3-12 months; a POTS-like autonomic picture has been described in prolonged post-COVID-19 (long COVID) syndromes.
Distinguishing IST from POTS is clinically critical because they require fundamentally different management approaches; conflating them risks worsening symptoms.
Asymptomatic sinus arrhythmia is physiologic, is not considered pathogenic, and does not warrant further cardiac evaluation.
harrison.pathophysiology: Sinus rhythm originates from spontaneous depolarization of pacemaker cells in the sinus node at the right atrium-SVC junction within the crista terminalis. Heart rate is modulated by the autonomic balance between sympathetic input (which accelerates and shifts the activation focus) and parasympathetic (vagal) input (which slows the node). Sinus arrhythmia reflects normal beat-to-beat shifts in autonomic tone, classically respiratory-linked vagal modulation. Sinus tachycardia results from increased sympathetic drive and/or vagal withdrawal raising the rate of spontaneous nodal depolarization; when this is an appropriate response to exercise, stress, or illness it is physiologic. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is thought to stem from an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic input to the node, altered membrane automaticity of sinus node cells, or both, though the precise mechanism remains poorly defined. POTS reflects orthostatic autonomic dysfunction, sometimes postviral.

Syncope or disabling palpitations accompanying tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia as a possible marker of underlying systemic illness (e.g., infection, malignancy, endocrine disorder) or drug toxicity
harrison.prognosis: Sinus arrhythmia is benign and physiologic, requiring no treatment. Physiologic sinus tachycardia resolves with correction of the underlying condition and often needs no specific therapy. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia tends to be a chronic, often disabling condition that responds poorly to therapy and may be difficult to control long term. POTS frequently improves over time, and postviral POTS may resolve spontaneously within 3-12 months.
pitfalls: Mislabeling rhythm irregularity with varying P-wave morphology as sinus arrhythmia when it is actually premature atrial contractions.
Diagnosing nonphysiologic sinus tachycardia before excluding reversible drivers such as anemia, thyroid disease, and pulmonary embolism.

Failing to separate inappropriate sinus tachycardia from POTS, since blood-pressure-raising strategies appropriate for POTS are inappropriate for IST, and sinus node modification is ineffective for POTS and may worsen its nontachycardia features.

Pursuing catheter-based sinus node modification for IST, which often yields poor long-term symptom control and can lead to symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, or chronotropic incompetence requiring a permanent pacemaker.
Overtreating an asymptomatic, constitutionally elevated resting or exercise sinus rate with no identifiable underlying cause.
harrison.severityClassification: Sinus tachycardia is rate-defined as >100 beats/min and sinus bradycardia as <60 beats/min, with normal sinus rhythm spanning 60-100 beats/min. POTS is defined diagnostically by an orthostatic heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (or to >120 beats/min) within 10 minutes of standing without hypotension. Sinus arrhythmia is defined by P-P interval variability >120 ms of sinus origin.
management: Reassure and observe benign physiological sinus arrhythmia and asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in fit or sleeping individuals, with no specific treatment
In physiological sinus tachycardia, identify and treat the underlying driver such as fever, sepsis, pain, hypovolaemia, anaemia or hyperthyroidism rather than the rate itself
Treat symptomatic inappropriate sinus tachycardia with a beta-blocker or the sinus-node current inhibitor ivabradine

Manage postural orthostatic tachycardia with increased salt and fluid intake, compression garments, graded exercise reconditioning and, if needed, a beta-blocker, ivabradine, fludrocortisone or midodrine
Correct reversible contributors including thyroid dysfunction and anaemia
Confirm the rhythm and distinguish it from paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with a 12-lead ECG and ambulatory telemetry
Refer for electrophysiology assessment and consideration of sinus-node modification in refractory, disabling inappropriate sinus tachycardia
Review culprit drugs and consider pacing for symptomatic pathological sinus bradycardia or sinus node dysfunction
